{
  "approach": "Model the 10 robots as a finite-source M/M/c/10 queue (Engset-like arrival process) in which each idle robot generates Poisson requests at rate 0.5/hr and each technician serves at rate 1/hr. Compute the steady-state blocking probability P_B = P(all c technicians busy | all busy robots attempting) for c = 1,2,... and pick the smallest c with P_B < 0.05.",
  "steps": [
    "Let N = 10 robots, lambda = 0.5 per idle robot per hour, mu = 1 per technician per hour, and c = number of technicians.",
    "Use the finite-source blocking formula: P_B = ( C(N-1, c) * (lambda/mu)^c ) / sum_{k=0}^{c} C(N-1, k) * (lambda/mu)^k, where C is the binomial coefficient. This is the Erlang-B-type formula adapted to finite population, giving the probability that all c technicians are busy given the state of the N-1 other robots.",
    "Alternatively, solve the full birth-death process with N total robots: states k = 0..N busy robots (in service), transition rates: from k to k+1 at (N-k)*lambda when k < c, and from k to k-1 at k*mu; state k = c..N have all technicians busy, so no new arrivals can start service (those requests are blocked). Compute steady-state probabilities and set P_B = sum_{k=c}^{N} pi_k.",
    "For each c = 1, 2, 3, ... compute P_B and find the smallest c such that P_B < 0.05.",
    "Verify the result using both the blocking formula and the full steady-state calculation; they should agree.",
    "Report the smallest c and its P_B in the steps/approach narrative (the JSON does not require a separate final answer field)."
  ],
  "critical_invariants": [
    "Arrival rate is 0.5 per hour per idle robot; the total arrival rate is (number of idle robots) * 0.5, not a fixed external rate.",
    "A blocked request occurs only when all c technicians are simultaneously busy; blocked requests are lost and do not affect robot idle status in that instant.",
    "A robot cannot originate a new request while already in a session: the service of that robot removes it from the idle population.",
    "Service times are exponential with mean 1 hour, so per-server service rate mu = 1/hour.",
    "Blocking probability must be strictly below 5% (0.05)."
  ],
  "assumptions": [
    "Technicians are distinguishable only by capacity; any idle technician can serve any robot.",
    "Robots are identical; their idle periods are independent exponential so the finite-source model is Markovian.",
    "The blocking probability is evaluated at steady state.",
    "The finite-source blocking formula above is correct for this system (to be verified against the full state solution)."
  ]
}
